title: Haemorrhoids
subject: Surgery
summary: Haemorrhoids are enlarged anal cushions that may bleed, thrombose or prolapse. Diagnosis is clinical, staging uses the Goligher system, and management ranges from lifestyle measures to surgery.

sections.p: Symptomatic enlargement and distal displacement of the anal vascular cushions. Diagnosis is made by history of painless bright‑red bleeding and visual inspection or proctoscopy.
b: Bright red per‑rectal bleed, no melena
Visible prolapse on straining
Tender perianal swelling suggests thrombosis

sections.p: Goligher classification grades internal haemorrhoids by degree of prolapse and reducibility.
b: Grade I: no prolapse
Grade II: prolapse on straining, reduces spontaneously
Grade III: prolapse on straining, reduces manually
Grade IV: prolapse, cannot be reduced

sections.p: Factors that raise intra‑abdominal pressure or impair venous return cause cushion engorgement.
b: Chronic constipation and low‑fibre diet
Prolonged straining on the toilet
Pregnancy and obesity
Portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis, schistosomiasis)
Heavy lifting, chronic cough

sections.p: Patients usually notice painless bright red bleeding, itching, or a prolapsing mass that may be painful if thrombosed.
b: Bleeding with bowel movements
Itching or irritation from mucus discharge
Painful lump if external thrombosis
Feeling of incomplete evacuation

t.b: Confirms internal haemorrhoids, grades prolapse, rules out fissure or tumour
Assesses external haemorrhoids, skin tags, and sphincter tone

t.a: Flexible sigmoidoscopy (if bleeding atypical or >50 y)
t.b: Excludes proximal colonic pathology such as cancer or inflammatory disease
Detects anemia from chronic blood loss; if unavailable, assess clinical pallor and fatigue

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but can be serious.
b: Severe anemia (Hb < 8 g/dL)
Thrombosed external haemorrhoid with increasing pain
Persistent bleeding despite conservative therapy
Signs of portal hypertension or rectal cancer

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, provide symptomatic relief, and consider surgery for high‑grade disease or failure of conservative care.
b: High‑fiber diet (≥25 g/day) and adequate hydration
Stool softeners (e.g., docusate) to avoid straining
Topical agents: witch‑hazel, lidocaine for pain/itch
Sitz baths 10‑15 min after defecation
Rubber band ligation for Grade II‑III internal disease
Excisional hemorrhoidectomy for Grade IV or recurrent disease
Avoid NSAIDs in active bleeding; prefer acetaminophen for pain

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 4‑6 weeks of conservative therapy; schedule surgical review if symptoms persist or worsen.
b: Re‑assess bleeding, prolapse, and pain
Re‑inforce diet, fluid, and bowel habits
Screen for portal hypertension in patients with liver disease

sections.p: Conditions that cause per‑rectal bleeding or perianal lumps.
b: Anal fissure – painful tear, posterior midline, sharp pain
Rectal prolapse – full‑thickness circumferential prolapse
Perianal abscess – tender, fluctuant, systemic signs
Colorectal cancer – occult bleeding, weight loss, mass

sections.p: Some investigations may appear normal despite significant disease.
b: Proctoscopy can miss small internal haemorrhoids if bowel not fully emptied
CBC may be normal in early chronic blood loss

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of infection: fever, increasing redness

faq.q: Why is bright red blood a clue to haemorrhoids?
faq.a: Bleeding from the distal anal canal is not digested, so it appears bright red and stains the stool or toilet paper.

faq.q: Can a low‑fiber diet cause haemorrhoids?
faq.a: Yes; hard stools increase straining, raising intra‑abdominal pressure and engorging the cushions.
For Grade IV disease, recurrent bleeding after ligation, or symptomatic external thrombosed haemorrhoids that do not resolve.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with painless bright red bleeding for 3 months; what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform proctoscopy to grade haemorrhoids and exclude fissure or tumour.

How does portal hypertension contribute to haemorrhoids and what extra investigation is warranted? — Increased portal pressure enlarges perianal collaterals; obtain ultrasound Doppler of portal system if liver disease suspected.

A patient with Grade III internal haemorrhoids refuses surgery; which office‑based treatment is appropriate and what are its contraindications? — Rubber band ligation; avoid if thrombosed external disease or anticoagulated with high bleeding risk.
Explain why stool softeners are preferred over bulk‑forming agents in acute haemorrhoid flare‑up. — Softeners reduce straining without increasing stool bulk that could worsen prolapse.
What feature distinguishes a thrombosed external haemorrhoid from an anal fissure on examination? — A tender, bluish perianal nodule versus a linear ulcer with spasm of the internal sphincter.

During a ward round you note a patient with chronic constipation, obesity, and bright red bleeding; what lifestyle advice would you give and what is the physiological rationale? — Increase fibre to ≥25 g/day, drink ≥2 L water, avoid prolonged toilet sitting; fibre softens stool and reduces intra‑abdominal pressure.

A patient with known cirrhosis presents with new perianal bleeding; how does management differ? — Assess for portal hypertension‑related varices, consider beta‑blocker therapy, and prioritize endoscopic surveillance of the oesophagus.
Why are NSAIDs avoided in a patient with active haemorrhoidal bleeding? — NSAIDs impair platelet function and can exacerbate mucosal bleeding.
